issues.legal_issue: Under the profits-basis method of assessing rateable value, the hypothetical rent is determined by reference to the premises’ profit-making capacity and the expenses properly incurred to earn the receipts.
material_facts: The assessment concerned a racecourse operated as a profit-making business, and the assessing authority used the profits-basis method based on the club’s accounts for the preceding year.
The club did not press its objection to use of that method, so the Court proceeded on the basis that it had been properly adopted.
issues.conclusion: The profits-basis method works from the business receipts, deducts the expenses properly incurred in earning them and other relevant deductions, and uses the resulting figure to indicate the rent a hypothetical tenant would pay; the profits themselves are not what is rated.
issues.legal_principle: Section 154(1) of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888 requires assessment by reference to the rent for which the property might reasonably be expected to let, less the statutory deduction. The Court applied the hypothetical landlord-and-tenant approach and described the profits-basis method as a way to indicate that rent from profit-making capacity. It referred to R. v. Verall, the Sandown Park case, and Port of London Authority v. Assessment Committee.

predicates.property_rating_assessment: The proceeding concerns determining the rateable value of property for property taxation.
predicates.profits_basis_method_used: The assessment uses the property’s receipts and expenditure to estimate the rent a hypothetical tenant would pay.

issues.definition: When a property-rating assessment uses the profits-basis method, its profit-making capacity and properly incurred receipt-earning expenses indicate the hypothetical rent.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s expenditure on maintaining a racecourse track as a source of business receipts is deductible separately from the statutory allowance for repairs and similar landlord expenses.
material_facts: The club incurred expenses to maintain the race track, which was a principal attraction for racegoers and participants and a source of the club’s receipts.
The lease excluded the relevant implied lessee obligation concerning repairs, but the disputed track expenses were not repairs to the leased land or the club’s structures.
The statutory deduction had been allowed in the assessment.
issues.conclusion: The track-maintenance expenses were proper business outgoings and could be deducted from gross receipts in addition to the statutory deduction; allowing them did not duplicate that deduction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 154(1) of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888 provides a ten-percent deduction in lieu of allowances for repairs or other matters, which the Court treated as covering costs incurred by the lessor. Applying the profits-basis method, expenses incurred by the tenant to maintain the course as a means of earning receipts were business outgoings, not part of that statutory allowance. The Court also considered section 108(m) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and the lease’s exclusion of the relevant implied covenant.

rule.if: property_rating_assessment and track_maintenance_expense and track_is_business_receipt_source and expense_is_tenant_business_outgoing

predicates.property_rating_assessment: The proceeding concerns determining the rateable value of property for property taxation.
predicates.track_maintenance_expense: The operating tenant incurred expenditure to maintain the track.
predicates.track_is_business_receipt_source: The track and its condition help the tenant earn business receipts from the premises.
predicates.expense_is_tenant_business_outgoing: The expenditure concerns the tenant’s business use of the premises rather than an obligation borne by the landlord.

issues.definition: If a tenant in a property-rating assessment incurs track-maintenance expenditure on a track that generates business receipts, and the expense is the tenant’s business outgoing, that expense is deducted separately from the statutory allowance.

issues.legal_issue: The cost of maintaining a totalisator that is a necessary adjunct to an efficiently operated racecourse is a deductible business outgoing even though the apparatus is machinery.
material_facts: The club incurred expenses to maintain and repair its totalisator, a mechanical device used to register and display betting operations.
The totalisator enabled races to be conducted efficiently and was an important adjunct to the racecourse.
issues.conclusion: The totalisator’s maintenance and repair expenses were business outgoings deductible in calculating rateable value under the profits-basis method; the contention based on the apparatus being machinery did not defeat the deduction.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 154(1) of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888, the profits-basis assessment takes account of expenses properly incurred to earn the receipts. The Court regarded upkeep of equipment necessary to an efficient racecourse as such an outgoing and rejected the argument based on the machinery provision in section 154(2).

rule.if: property_rating_assessment and profits_basis_method_used and equipment_maintenance_expense and equipment_is_necessary_business_adjunct

predicates.property_rating_assessment: The proceeding concerns determining the rateable value of property for property taxation.
predicates.profits_basis_method_used: The assessment uses the property’s receipts and expenditure to estimate the rent a hypothetical tenant would pay.
predicates.equipment_maintenance_expense: The tenant incurred expenditure to maintain or repair equipment used in operating the business.
predicates.equipment_is_necessary_business_adjunct: The equipment is an important or necessary adjunct to operating the business efficiently and earning receipts.

issues.definition: In a property-rating assessment using the profits-basis method, expenditure to maintain equipment that is a necessary business adjunct is deductible.

issues.legal_issue: Business expenses for maintaining and operating premises are not apportioned to the landlord merely because the business uses the premises for only part of the year, absent a basis for treating the landlord as responsible during the remainder.
material_facts: The club incurred expenses for sand and moorum, employees, motor vehicles, stores and animal maintenance, garden work, machinery parts, wheel tax, and water tax.
Race meetings were held at the course for only part of the year.
Nothing in the lease showed that the lessor had to maintain the track during the period when meetings were not held there.
issues.conclusion: The entire amount of the relevant expenses could be deducted; the expenses could not be apportioned between tenant and landlord merely because race meetings were held for only part of the year.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 154(1) of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888, the profits-basis method requires deduction of expenses reasonably and properly incurred to earn receipts. The duration of the business’s active season alone does not transfer the tenant’s continuing maintenance obligations to the landlord.

rule.if: property_rating_assessment and profits_basis_method_used and business_maintenance_expenses and business_uses_premises_part_year and landlord_maintenance_obligation_not_shown

predicates.property_rating_assessment: The proceeding concerns determining the rateable value of property for property taxation.
predicates.profits_basis_method_used: The assessment uses the property’s receipts and expenditure to estimate the rent a hypothetical tenant would pay.
predicates.business_maintenance_expenses: The tenant incurred expenses for maintaining or operating the premises and its business facilities.
predicates.business_uses_premises_part_year: The business holds its principal events or conducts its principal activity at the premises for only part of the year.
predicates.landlord_maintenance_obligation_not_show: The lease or other evidence does not establish that the landlord must bear the relevant maintenance expenses during the rest of the year.

issues.definition: When a business in a profits-basis property-rating assessment uses the premises for only part of the year, its maintenance expenses are not seasonally apportioned to the landlord unless a landlord maintenance obligation is shown.

issues.legal_issue: A licence fee paid by the tenant to obtain permission to conduct races is the tenant’s business expense and is not divided with the landlord as a fee for licensing the premises.
material_facts: The club’s committee applied for and obtained a licence permitting the club to hold races on two courses, and the committee acted on behalf of the club.
The licence authorized the conduct of races; it was not an instrument licensing the premises as a racecourse.
The applicable legislation contained no provision establishing a separate licence fee for the premises.
issues.conclusion: The club was entitled to deduct the entire licence fee allocated to the course in issue as its own business expense; the fee was not to be split between tenant and landlord.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3 and 4 of the Bombay Race-Courses Licensing Act, 1912 prohibit racing without the required licence and provide for a licence for horse racing. The Court held that the fee was payable by the person conducting the racing business, not by the landlord, and found no statutory basis for treating the licence as having a dual purpose of licensing both the premises and the operator.

predicates.property_rating_assessment: The proceeding concerns determining the rateable value of property for property taxation.
predicates.race_business_licence_fee: A fee was paid to obtain a licence connected with racing conducted on the premises.
predicates.licence_authorizes_tenant_to_conduct_rac: The licence authorizes the tenant or its agent to conduct races rather than licensing the premises as such.
predicates.premises_licence_fee_not_separately_prov: The governing scheme does not provide for a separate fee for licensing the premises.

issues.definition: If a tenant pays a racing licence fee to obtain permission to conduct races and no separate premises-licensing fee is provided, the entire fee is the tenant’s expense.

issues.legal_issue: Rateable value based on the rent a hypothetical tenant would pay need not equal the actual rent payable under the existing lease.
material_facts: The High Court’s rateable-value calculation resulted in a figure below the actual rent payable under the lease.
The club had exclusive possession of only some portions of the land, while the remainder had to be kept open to the public except on race days and during horse training.
issues.conclusion: Rateable value need not equal actual rent; it is measured by the rent a hypothetical tenant would pay for the property as it exists, taking account of its advantages and burdens.
issues.legal_principle: Section 154(1) of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888 requires a hypothetical annual-rent assessment rather than adoption of the actual rent. The relevant measure considers the property’s privileges, advantages, and burdens, including restrictions on exclusive possession.

rule.if: property_rating_assessment and hypothetical_rent_method_applied and actual_lease_rent_differs and property_use_restricted

predicates.property_rating_assessment: The proceeding concerns determining the rateable value of property for property taxation.
predicates.hypothetical_rent_method_applied: The assessment estimates the rent a hypothetical tenant would pay for the property as it exists.
predicates.actual_lease_rent_differs: The rent under the actual lease differs from the amount produced by the assessment.
predicates.property_use_restricted: The tenant’s exclusive use of the property is limited by conditions requiring some portions to remain available for public or other use.

issues.definition: Where a property-rating assessment uses hypothetical rent and the property’s use is restricted, a difference between the assessed value and actual lease rent does not require the assessed value to equal that rent.
